name: Battle of Zama

phases.title: The armies draw up facing each other
phases.text: The Romans put their heavy infantry in the centre in three ranks, with Laelius's cavalry on the left and Masinissa's Numidians on the right. Hannibal set elephants before two lines of infantry, a third line well behind them, and cavalry on each flank.

phases.title: The Numidian horsemen skirmish on the flank
phases.text: The first clashes came on the Carthaginian left and the Roman right, between the Numidian cavalry on the Carthaginian side and those siding with the Romans. Each force sent detachments to hurl javelins at the other and then withdraw.

phases.title: The elephants charge with two lines behind them
phases.text: Hannibal ordered his 80 elephants to charge the Roman infantry, with the whole of his first two infantry lines moving forward in support. His third line stayed where it stood.

phases.title: The velites and the bugles turn the elephants
phases.text: The velites moved forward, threw javelins at the elephants and fell back, and the Roman heavy infantry sounded their bugles. Many elephants bolted, most into the gaps the Romans had left between their maniples.

phases.title: Masinissa routs the Numidian cavalry
phases.text: Elephants that fled trampled through the Numidian cavalry on the Carthaginian side and disordered it. Masinissa ordered a charge, which routed those horsemen, and his force pursued them.

phases.title: Laelius routs the African cavalry
phases.text: Elephants that fled disorganised the Carthaginian cavalry on the other wing. Laelius ordered his cavalry to charge, and the Carthaginian cavalry was swept from the field with the Roman cavalry close behind.

phases.title: The first lines of infantry clash
phases.text: With elephants and cavalry gone from the field, all three Roman ranks and the first two Carthaginian ranks advanced and met in close, hand-to-hand fighting. The Carthaginian third rank, the veterans from Italy, remained in place.

phases.title: The Carthaginian front line breaks
phases.text: The Romans' superior weapons and organisation told, though the hastati took further heavy losses, and the Carthaginian front rank broke and fled. The second rank would not let them through, so they escaped round its flanks.

phases.title: The second line pushes the Romans back
phases.text: The hastati then attacked the Carthaginian second rank. Its African spearmen fought fanatically, and the Romans were pushed back in disorder.

phases.title: The Romans commit the principes
phases.text: The Romans were forced to commit their second line, the principes, to the fight. Even they struggled to hold the line at first, but their reinforcement was enough to break the Carthaginian second line.

phases.title: The second line flees and the hastati pursue
phases.text: The Carthaginian second line broke and fled, pursued impetuously by the hastati. The Carthaginian third line did not move.

phases.title: Both sides re-form into single long lines
phases.text: The Romans recalled the hastati and formed one line, with the principes and triarii at the sides. The Carthaginians rallied survivors of their first two lines to lengthen the veterans' line, so it outflanked the Romans.

phases.title: The two single lines charge each other
phases.text: Having re-formed, the two lines charged each other with, in Polybius's words, the greatest fire and fury. The fight continued for some time and neither side gained the advantage.

phases.title: The Roman cavalry returns and takes the line in the rear
phases.text: Masinissa's and Laelius's cavalry returned to the battlefield at more or less the same time. The Carthaginian infantry, fiercely engaged to their front, could not prevent a charge into their rear, and their line collapsed.

note: The accounts give no directions, so the Romans are drawn on the left facing right. The accounts give no ground for the fight beyond a flat area, so none is drawn. The Roman velites stood in avenues between the maniples; they are drawn as one small block in front of the hastati, as the accounts do not say exactly where they stood. The Carthaginian light infantry and the 6,000 Numidian infantry on the Roman side are not drawn: the accounts do not say where the second stood, and the first screened the elephants. The Roman heavy infantry are drawn as hastati, principes and triarii, without the allied legions on each side. Which of the principes and triarii went to which side when the single line formed is not stated; they are drawn one to each side. Before the last fight the survivors of the Carthaginian first and second lines are drawn extending the line of the third. Polybius is the main source for the battle; the later accounts of Livy and Appian differ from it and are not followed.
